topicName: Storage Engine: Pages, Extents, and Allocation Units
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding SQL Server Storage Engine: Pages, Extents, and Allocation Units"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"At the core of Microsoft SQL Server lies the storage engine, responsible for managing how data is written to and read from physical disk storage. To optimize input/output (I/O) operations, SQL Server does not manage data at the individual byte level. Instead, it organizes storage hierarchically using Pages, Extents, and Allocation Units."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Data Pages"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The fundamental unit of data storage in SQL Server is a page. A page has a fixed size of 8 KB (8,192 bytes). This means SQL Server can allocate and read 8 KB of data in a single disk I/O operation. Out of the 8 KB, the first 96 bytes are reserved for a header that stores metadata about the page, such as the page type, amount of free space, and the page ID."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Data Page: Contains the actual table or index rows."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Index Page: Contains index entries that point to data pages."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"GAM/SGAM Pages: Track the allocation status of extents (Global Allocation Map and Shared Global Allocation Map)."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Extents"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"An extent is a collection of 8 contiguous pages, making an extent 64 KB in size. SQL Server manages space in extents rather than individual pages to ensure efficient allocation. There are two types of extents in SQL Server:"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Uniform Extents: Owned by a single object (like a specific table or index). All 8 pages within a uniform extent belong exclusively to that object."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Mixed Extents: Shared by up to 8 different objects. Small tables or indexes initially store their first few pages in mixed extents to save space before graduating to uniform extents."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Allocation Units"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Allocation units are collections of pages used to manage data based on their type. When a table or index grows, SQL Server uses three types of allocation units to manage the underlying pages:"},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"IN_ROW_DATA: Contains the actual data rows for the table or index (excluding LOB data)."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"LOB_DATA: Stores Large Object (LOB) data types such as VARCHAR(MAX), VARBINARY(MAX), XML, and TEXT."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ROW_OVERFLOW_DATA: Stores variable-length data (VARCHAR, NVARCHAR, VARBINARY) that exceeds the 8,060-byte row size limit within the IN_ROW_DATA allocation unit."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Inspect Page and Extent Usage via T-SQL"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can inspect the physical page and extent allocation of your tables and indexes using the system catalog view sys.allocation_units and sys.dm_db_database_page_allocations. Below is a sample query to check the allocation units for a specific table:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"SELECT 
    t.name AS TableName,
    au.type_desc AS AllocationUnitType,
    au.total_pages AS TotalPages,
    au.used_pages AS UsedPages,
    (au.total_pages * 8) / 1024 AS TotalSizeMB
FROM sys.tables t
INNER JOIN sys.partitions p ON t.object_id = p.object_id
INNER JOIN sys.allocation_units au ON p.partition_id = au.container_id
WHERE t.name = 'YourTableName';"}]
